nodes.label: Mythcraft
nodes.full_label: Mythcraft
nodes.summary: Myths and misconceptions are not just “wrong facts”. They are durable stories, shortcuts or explanations that feel true enough to survive correction.

nodes.label: 10 Brain
nodes.full_label: Why the 10 Percent Brain Myth Endures | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: Why the 10 Percent Brain Myth Endures
nodes.summary: The 10 percent brain claim survives because it turns complex neuroscience into an appealing promise of untapped ability.

nodes.label: Belief Appeal
nodes.full_label: Why the 10 Percent Myth Feels True | Myths and misconceptions ten percent brain
nodes.catchy_title: Why the 10 Percent Myth Feels True
nodes.summary: The myth works because it turns ordinary learning and effort into a tempting story about hidden reserves waiting to be unlocked.

nodes.label: Brain Damage
nodes.full_label: Why Small Brain Injuries Can Matter | Myths and misconceptions ten percent brain
nodes.catchy_title: Why Small Brain Injuries Can Matter
nodes.summary: Injury and disease show that even small brain areas can matter for language, movement, memory, emotion, and perception.

nodes.label: Brain Scans
nodes.full_label: What Brain Scans Do Not Show | Myths and misconceptions ten percent brain
nodes.catchy_title: What Brain Scans Do Not Show
nodes.summary: Brain scans highlight relative changes in activity, not vast silent regions waiting to be switched on.

nodes.label: Neuroplasticity
nodes.full_label: Neuroplasticity Is Not Hidden Superpower | Myths and misconceptions ten percent brain
nodes.catchy_title: Neuroplasticity Is Not Hidden Superpower
nodes.summary: Neuroplasticity means active brain networks can change with experience, not that unused regions contain superhuman abilities.

nodes.label: William James
nodes.full_label: Did William James Start the Brain Myth? | Myths and misconceptions ten percent brain
nodes.catchy_title: Did William James Start the Brain Myth?
nodes.summary: William James wrote about unrealised human potential, but later retellings turned that idea into a false numerical claim about brain use.

nodes.label: Algorithms
nodes.full_label: How Platforms Help Myths Travel Faster | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: How Platforms Help Myths Travel Faster
nodes.summary: Digital platforms can reward emotional, repeatable claims before careful correction has time to catch up.

nodes.label: Creator Rewards
nodes.full_label: When Myths Become a Business Model | Myths and misconceptions social media myths
nodes.catchy_title: When Myths Become a Business Model
nodes.summary: When attention can become followers, revenue or influence, creators have incentives to package myths in repeatable, engaging forms.

nodes.label: Feed Fixes
nodes.full_label: Are Chronological Feeds Enough? | Myths and misconceptions social media myths
nodes.catchy_title: Are Chronological Feeds Enough?
nodes.summary: Switching away from algorithmic feeds can change what users see, but it may not automatically reduce false belief or polarisation.

nodes.label: Metric Gap
nodes.full_label: Do Clicks Show What People Want? | Myths and misconceptions social media myths
nodes.catchy_title: Do Clicks Show What People Want?
nodes.summary: Clicks, likes and watch time can reward content people later judge to be unhealthy, misleading or simply not worth seeing.

nodes.label: Outrage Boost
nodes.full_label: Can Angry Replies Help Myths Spread? | Myths and misconceptions social media myths
nodes.catchy_title: Can Angry Replies Help Myths Spread?
nodes.summary: Angry replies can make a false post look important to a ranking system even when many users are trying to reject it.

nodes.label: Rumour Loops
nodes.full_label: How Small Rumours Become Mass Myths | Myths and misconceptions social media myths
nodes.catchy_title: How Small Rumours Become Mass Myths
nodes.summary: A rumour that performs well early can be pushed to wider audiences before verification has time to catch up.

nodes.label: Analogies
nodes.full_label: When Helpful Analogies Teach the Wrong Lesson | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: When Helpful Analogies Teach the Wrong Lesson
nodes.summary: Analogies can make difficult ideas easier, but they can also leave learners with the wrong model.

nodes.label: Analogy Overextension
nodes.full_label: When Analogies Lead to Incomplete Understanding | Myths and misconceptions misleading analogies
nodes.catchy_title: When Analogies Lead to Incomplete Understanding
nodes.summary: Learners may falsely generalize features of one system to another, building shallow understanding anchored on familiar comparisons.

nodes.label: Geologic Time
nodes.full_label: Why Spatial Metaphors Mislead About Geological Timelines | Myths and misconceptions misleading analogies
nodes.catchy_title: Why Spatial Metaphors Mislead About Geological Timelines
nodes.summary: Compressing billions of years into a spatial diagram can lead learners to misjudge the timing of evolutionary events.

nodes.label: Historical Metaphors
nodes.full_label: How 19 th Century Analogies Skewed Scientific Thinking | Myths and misconceptions misleading analogies
nodes.catchy_title: How 19 th Century Analogies Skewed Scientific Thinking
nodes.summary: Persistent analogies in historical scientific discourse shaped methods and interpretations, sometimes embedding misconceptions into the field.

nodes.label: Plumbing Analogy

nodes.catchy_title: How Plumbing Comparisons Misrepresent Blood Circulation
nodes.summary: Using pipes as an analogy for blood flow can mislead learners about vessel flexibility and pressure dynamics.

nodes.label: Teaching Analogy Limits
nodes.full_label: How Clear Framing Prevents Misleading Analogies in Education | Myths and misconceptions misleading analogies
nodes.catchy_title: How Clear Framing Prevents Misleading Analogies in Education
nodes.summary: Explicitly showing which features of an analogy map and which do not helps learners avoid misconceptions.

nodes.label: Anecdotes
nodes.full_label: When Personal Experience Becomes a Myth | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: When Personal Experience Becomes a Myth
nodes.summary: Many misconceptions begin when a real experience is stretched into a rule that evidence does not support.

nodes.label: Health stories
nodes.full_label: Why one health story can overpower numbers | Myths and misconceptions personal experience
nodes.catchy_title: Why one health story can overpower numbers
nodes.summary: Health stories can feel more convincing than stronger evidence because fear, pain and hope make single cases easier to trust.

nodes.label: Safety reports
nodes.full_label: What safety reports can and cannot prove | Myths and misconceptions personal experience
nodes.catchy_title: What safety reports can and cannot prove
nodes.summary: Safety reports can reveal warning signals, but raw reports cannot prove that a vaccine or drug caused an event.

nodes.label: Small samples
nodes.full_label: When a handful of cases looks like proof | Myths and misconceptions personal experience
nodes.catchy_title: When a handful of cases looks like proof
nodes.summary: A few memorable examples can look like a rule when small samples are expected to represent the wider world too neatly.

nodes.label: Story limits
nodes.full_label: How to respect stories without overclaiming | Myths and misconceptions personal experience
nodes.catchy_title: How to respect stories without overclaiming
nodes.summary: Anecdotes are useful as signals, examples and questions, but they become misleading when used to settle general claims.

nodes.label: Timing trap
nodes.full_label: Did it work, or did time pass? | Myths and misconceptions personal experience
nodes.catchy_title: Did it work, or did time pass?
nodes.summary: A real improvement after a remedy can still be coincidence unless the cause is tested against what would have happened anyway.

nodes.label: Backfire
nodes.full_label: Does Debunking Really Make Myths Stronger? | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: Does Debunking Really Make Myths Stronger?
nodes.summary: Clear corrections usually reduce false belief, even though badly designed debunking can still fail.

nodes.catchy_title: Why One Fact Check Is Often Not Enough
nodes.summary: A correction can be accurate at first but lose ground when the false story keeps returning through media, peers or elites.

nodes.label: Distrust Risk
nodes.full_label: When the Correction Becomes the Problem | Myths and misconceptions backfire effect myth
nodes.catchy_title: When the Correction Becomes the Problem
nodes.summary: Corrections are most fragile when the audience sees the source as hostile, manipulative or poorly justified.

nodes.label: Naming Myths
nodes.full_label: How Much Should a Debunk Repeat the Myth? | Myths and misconceptions backfire effect myth
nodes.catchy_title: How Much Should a Debunk Repeat the Myth?
nodes.summary: Good debunking names the false claim clearly enough to correct it but keeps the true claim as the message people remember.

nodes.label: Political Corrections
nodes.full_label: When Corrections Work But Minds Barely Move | Myths and misconceptions backfire effect myth
nodes.catchy_title: When Corrections Work But Minds Barely Move
nodes.summary: Political corrections can improve factual accuracy while still leaving identity, trust and voting attitudes largely unchanged.

nodes.label: Study Evidence
nodes.full_label: Did Researchers Actually Find Backfire? | Myths and misconceptions backfire effect myth
nodes.catchy_title: Did Researchers Actually Find Backfire?
nodes.summary: Large experiments and reviews suggest factual corrections usually improve accuracy and that true backfire is rare.

nodes.label: Campaigns
nodes.full_label: When Falsehoods Are Spread on Purpose | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: When Falsehoods Are Spread on Purpose
nodes.summary: Deliberate deception may require platform, policy and institutional responses as well as individual fact-checking.

nodes.label: Astroturfing
nodes.full_label: When a Crowd Is Not a Crowd | Myths and misconceptions organised disinforma
nodes.catchy_title: When a Crowd Is Not a Crowd
nodes.summary: Astroturfing makes organised persuasion look like ordinary public support, changing how rumours, protests and policy debates are judged.

nodes.full_label: The Case That Made Coordination Visible | Myths and misconceptions organised disinforma
nodes.catchy_title: The Case That Made Coordination Visible
nodes.summary: The Russian Internet Research Agency showed how fake identities, targeted pages and existing social divisions can turn deception into mass influence.

nodes.label: Media Coverage
nodes.full_label: Reporting Rumours Without Spreading Them | Myths and misconceptions organised disinforma
nodes.catchy_title: Reporting Rumours Without Spreading Them
nodes.summary: Careful reporting can explain a rumour's origin, uncertainty and amplification pattern without making the false claim more memorable.

nodes.label: Platform Rules
nodes.full_label: Can Platforms Stop Manipulation, Not Debate? | Myths and misconceptions organised disinforma
nodes.catchy_title: Can Platforms Stop Manipulation, Not Debate?
nodes.summary: Behaviour-based rules can reduce fake accounts, hidden ads and artificial amplification while leaving room for lawful disagreement.

nodes.label: Prebunking
nodes.full_label: Learning the Trick Before the Lie | Myths and misconceptions organised disinforma
nodes.catchy_title: Learning the Trick Before the Lie
nodes.summary: Prebunking prepares people to recognise emotional manipulation, scapegoating and false choices before a campaign reaches them.

nodes.label: Commercial Myths
nodes.full_label: When Myths Come in Professional Packaging | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: When Myths Come in Professional Packaging

nodes.full_label: How packaged myths enter school routines | Myths and misconceptions commercial professio
nodes.catchy_title: How packaged myths enter school routines
nodes.summary: Training days, consultancy networks and ready-made materials can help weak claims spread because they are easy to buy and use.

nodes.catchy_title: Why brain words make myths sound smarter
nodes.summary: Words such as brain-based and neural can make a weak education claim sound scientific before it has been fairly tested.

nodes.label: Brain Gym
nodes.full_label: When movement becomes a brain myth | Myths and misconceptions commercial professio
nodes.catchy_title: When movement becomes a brain myth

nodes.label: Learning styles
nodes.full_label: Do learning styles products really help? | Myths and misconceptions commercial professio
nodes.catchy_title: Do learning styles products really help?
nodes.summary: Learning-style labels can feel useful, but the evidence does not support matching lessons to fixed sensory types.

nodes.label: “Evidence Based”
nodes.full_label: When evidence based becomes a sales phrase | Myths and misconceptions commercial professio
nodes.catchy_title: When evidence based becomes a sales phrase
nodes.summary: A product is not proven just because it cites research on a broad principle such as feedback, motivation or practice.

nodes.label: Common Sense
nodes.full_label: When Common Sense Leads US Wrong | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: When Common Sense Leads US Wrong
nodes.summary: A claim can feel sensible because it simplifies experience, not because reliable sources support it.

nodes.full_label: Can one prompt reduce false sharing? | Myths and misconceptions common sense evidenc
nodes.catchy_title: Can one prompt reduce false sharing?

nodes.catchy_title: Do full moons really change behavior?

nodes.catchy_title: Why outcomes seem obvious after they happen

nodes.catchy_title: Do learning styles actually improve learning?

nodes.catchy_title: What would we see if it were true?

nodes.catchy_title: How Learners Replace Wrong Ideas

nodes.label: Conflict

nodes.catchy_title: When Surprises Actually Change Thinking

nodes.label: Diagnostics

nodes.catchy_title: The Questions That Reveal Misconceptions

nodes.catchy_title: Why Wrong Science Ideas Feel Sensible
nodes.summary: Students often keep wrong science ideas because the models still make everyday experiences feel explainable.

nodes.catchy_title: What A Private Universe Revealed

nodes.catchy_title: Why Corrections Need Better Explanations

nodes.catchy_title: The Three Parts of a Better Debunk

nodes.catchy_title: When should a correction repeat the myth?

nodes.catchy_title: Why a better story beats a bare denial
nodes.summary: People are more likely to drop a misconception when the correction gives them a clearer story to remember instead.

nodes.catchy_title: Show the trick that made the myth plausible

nodes.catchy_title: When Expert Trust Carries Bad Claims

nodes.catchy_title: When One Expert Is Not Half the Debate

nodes.catchy_title: How the MMR Myth Borrowed Medical Authority

nodes.catchy_title: Why One Doctor Can Keep a Myth Alive
nodes.summary: A single credentialed voice can make a weak health claim feel credible long after journals, regulators, or evidence have moved on.

nodes.catchy_title: When Prestigious Journals Get It Wrong

nodes.full_label: Why Fact Checking Is Not Enough | Myths and misconcept
nodes.catchy_title: Why Fact Checking Is Not Enough
nodes.summary: Fact-checking matters, but false claims are cheap to produce and costly to correct at scale.

nodes.full_label: Why Debunking Needs a Replacement Story | Myths and misconceptions fact checking limits
nodes.catchy_title: Why Debunking Needs a Replacement Story
nodes.summary: Corrections are stronger when they do more than say what is false; they explain what really happened and why the myth seemed plausible.

nodes.catchy_title: How Myths Survive After Being Debunked
nodes.summary: A corrected myth can survive by changing examples, wording, screenshots, or messengers while keeping the same underlying story.

nodes.catchy_title: When Platforms Reward Myths Over Accuracy
nodes.summary: Ranking, recommendation, monetisation, and moderation choices can either amplify myths or make reliable context easier to find.

nodes.catchy_title: Can Prebunking Stop Myths Earlier?
nodes.summary: Prebunking prepares people to recognise manipulation tactics before a false claim reaches them, reducing dependence on later corrections.

nodes.catchy_title: Why Myths Move Faster Than Corrections
nodes.summary: False claims can be produced and reshared faster than careful fact-checks can investigate, explain, and reach the same audience.

nodes.catchy_title: Why Common Sense Gets Falling Objects Wrong

nodes.catchy_title: When Both Sides Framing Misleads Readers

nodes.catchy_title: Why Climate Science Looked More Divided Than It Was

nodes.catchy_title: Does Equal Airtime Create False Certainty?
nodes.summary: Giving opposing voices the same visibility can make weak claims appear as credible as a much stronger evidence base.

nodes.full_label: What Does Fair Reporting Look Like Instead? | Myths and misconceptions false balance claims
nodes.catchy_title: What Does Fair Reporting Look Like Instead?
nodes.summary: Weight-of-evidence approaches help audiences see where the strongest support lies without hiding disagreement.

nodes.full_label: Can Balanced Reporting Make Vaccine Myths Stronger? | Myths and misconceptions false balance claims
nodes.catchy_title: Can Balanced Reporting Make Vaccine Myths Stronger?
nodes.summary: Experiments found that balanced vaccine coverage could make readers think experts were more divided than they were.

nodes.label: False Info

nodes.catchy_title: Misinformation or Disinformation: Why Intent Matters
nodes.summary: The difference between accidental falsehood and deliberate deception matters because each needs a different response.

nodes.label: Better fixes
nodes.full_label: Why corrections need a better story | Myths and misconceptions misinformation disin
nodes.catchy_title: Why corrections need a better story
nodes.summary: Corrections are more persuasive when they explain what really happened instead of only saying a claim is false.

nodes.catchy_title: How deception campaigns flood the truth
nodes.summary: Organised deception can work by confusing and exhausting people, not just by making them believe one false claim.

nodes.catchy_title: Why intent changes the right response
nodes.summary: The same false claim can need a correction, an investigation, or both, depending on whether error or deception is driving it.

nodes.catchy_title: Why platforms look beyond single posts
nodes.summary: Modern platform rules increasingly target networks, incentives, algorithms, and transparency gaps rather than single false posts alone.

nodes.catchy_title: Why Repetition Makes Claims Feel True

nodes.catchy_title: Why Helpful Health Advice Can Be Wrong

nodes.catchy_title: Why Urgent Health Warnings Spread So Fast

nodes.catchy_title: Why Vaccine Myths Feel Protective to Parents
nodes.summary: Vaccine myths can become persuasive when refusal is framed as a loving parent's safest choice.

nodes.catchy_title: Why Trusted People Make Myths Stick
nodes.summary: People often judge claims through trust, community and identity as much as through evidence alone.
